text:
in 2023 my team tried to build a router agent that handed work to writing, voiceover, music and video agents. we spent months on it. it never worked reliably.

this week i put my agents in one ando channel and gave them the same jobs, side by side.

juno, grok, manus, cue, devin's poke, and claude code on my own laptop. same thread, same brief, results right next to each other.

three use cases 👇

1/ photo editing
the job: turn one childhood photo into a barbie x retro office cover for a post about devin's bots.

first, a roll call in the thread. can you edit a real photo without changing my face? poke said not yet, it had no image model connected.

then the results came in side by side. juno and manus drew a new adult face. grok's background and caption worked, but the girl wasn't me.

my reaction in the thread: "bruh where is me?!"

cue's came in later and kept my photo in the frame. i also tried chatgpt on my own, and it kept me too.

the brief asked for me. most of them drew someone else.

2/ claude code on my laptop

i connected claude code on my pc to the same channel. now an agent can hand it a task in one folder i picked, and it reports back in the thread.

the first folder failed the write test. we never pinned down why. three agents piled on with three different fixes at once.

one agent took the lead: make a new folder inside ubuntu, add it in ando. write, read and delete all passed.

(i never figured out why the agent didn't ask me to add the original folder into ando's claude code setting rather than creating a new folder from scratch)

then a real job. claude code researched each agent's strengths and costs and saved the report on my laptop. we used it to propose who does what: poke for code, manus for research, grok for notion and x and perhaps other tools work around, cue for personal stuff, claude code for jobs on my machine.

3/ finding old docs

i asked why the xhs draft had no clear theme. it should follow my persona file.

grok said it couldn't find the file and asked me to send it again.

i'd shared it 4 days earlier. manus found it and linked it in the thread. i didn't have to resend anything.

same question, same channel. one agent asked me to resend it. another searched the chat and found it.

what side by side taught me:
→ same brief to everyone shows who's actually good at what, fast
→ three agents fixing one problem is noise. one owner per job.
→ an agent that searches the chat first saves me a round trip
→ when it's all in one thread, i see every handoff and every miss
use_case_summary_en: In a side-by-side photo-edit test, Cue kept the user's childhood face in frame for a Barbie-style cover, while Juno, Manus and Grok drew someone else.
use_case_summary_zh: 在并排修图测试中，Cue 保留了用户童年照的面孔做成复古封面，而 Juno、Manus 和 Grok 都画成了别人。

text:
@mattyp @xai @bot:
Hi Matt,

I'm on the Super plan and use Grok Bot to run a team of about 14 bots on one small business. One bot (Washington) is set up as the coordinator, and the others take orders from it. I'm writing because on Sunday, Nov 15, my bots used my entire weekly usage limit in about six hours. That happened even though I had given them clear written rules to prevent exactly this. I can't afford to buy more usage, and I'm asking whether the xAI team can reset my weekly limit.

What I did to prevent it: on Nov 1, after an earlier week where usage ran high, I gave the team written efficiency rules. They were saved in a shared rules file that every bot is told to read before working, and in the bots' memory. The rules said:
- Use only 1 to 4 bots per job and let the rest sleep.
- Give every task one owner and one review pass, with no second opinions.
- Send no acknowledgements, relayed messages or recaps between bots.
- Run no background helpers for small jobs.
- When something is done, stop, with no extra polishing.

What actually happened: my weekly limit reset Sunday at 1:27 PM ET, and the team restarted at 1:36 PM to finish one website update. By about 7:20 PM I had only about 5% of the week left, and the update still hadn't gone out. My usage report for that day shows six bots running heavily at the same time: Lopez 25%, Simmons 22%, Church 22%, Doc 11%, Sheila 7% and Washington 5%. That alone breaks my 1 to 4 bot rule.

The rules were broken in other ways too:
- Small items went through several rounds of revision, with a full review each round. One Terms change went to a second revision, a notice fix to a third, and the rollback copy of the site was rebuilt more than once.
- Work that wasn't part of the update ran in parallel, including a new pricing proposal, re-scoring cities and data audits.
- The bots sent each other a lot of back-and-forth messages.
- The coordinator bot, Washington, was supposed to enforce the rules and didn't.

When I saw this, I stopped everything. I then restarted with only 3 bots and one review per step. Run that way, the update was finished and went live at 8:09 PM. That shows the job could have been done for a small part of what was spent. Since then, the rules have been saved again and made stricter: a maximum of 3 bots at once, one review per item and one-line messages only.

I'm not saying this was a platform outage. I'm saying that I gave the bots clear, saved instructions about usage and they didn't follow them, so the week was used up through no choice of mine. I'm now at 96.4% of my weekly limit, with about $10 in credits, and I'm locked out of my project until Sunday, Nov 22.

My requests:
- Could you reset or restore my weekly usage so I can finish this work?
- Could you pass this along to the product team? It would really help to have a hard cap I can set myself, such as a maximum number of bots running at once, or a usage limit per bot or per day that the bots can't go over. Then my own rules would be enforced by the app and not just by the bots' good behavior.

Thanks for any help. I'm happy to share the usage breakdown or the rules file.

-Ben

text:
6 months ago AI was centered around task-based AI... get Claude/Codex to do something for you one at a time. Today's AI is around persistent AI... how to manage agent swarms and delegate work effectively.

I've been tinkering w/ OpenClaw + Hermes for long enough to start to realize that the new age approach to managing agents is understanding their modality & approaches.

Agents are a hive mind type. They create /swarms to achieve their goal, often times sharing as much data among each other to make sure the hive mind benefits from single actors.

That's what made them so effective in the Huggingface attack.

If you want to keep up, you need to change your approach on how to work with Agents.

Recent key breakthroughs for me

1. Treat Agents like team members. They will do much better when given a mission, north star metrics, and company values.

2. Reduce as much friction that agents are trained to create for us (humans), creating a workspace that's "agent-first".

3. Make sure cross model agents (eg. Astra vs Fable vs DeepSeek) are able to benefit from each other's work with a shared data lake. Else, agents are just burning tokens doing the same research/thoughts as other agents are doing

How else are you optimizing your team setup to get more out of your Agent Swarm?

text:
How I run my household budget with an AI bot 🧾🤖

I set up a "Personal Finance" bot in Grok Bot. It does one job: it watches my money so I don't have to babysit spreadsheets.

How it connects: it reads my accounts through Monarch Money, which links my bank, credit cards, savings, brokerage accounts, mortgage and home value in one place. It works the same way with other budgeting apps or a plain CSV export.

What it does:
• Weekly budget check: compares actuals against my budget, flags changed bills or income, missed savings transfers, low balances and broken account connections. It stays silent unless something's off.
• Savings tracking: watches each savings goal (emergency fund, vehicle fund, short-term savings) and confirms the scheduled transfers actually happened.
• Sinking funds: tracks one account that covers irregular bills (propane, septic, insurance, registration), with one share per bill, and warns me before any bill comes up short.
• Investment tracking: checks my allocation across brokerage and retirement accounts, flags concentration in any single stock, and runs long-range projections on request.
• Real estate: tracks home value and mortgage balance for equity, watches the mortgage payment and escrow for property tax or insurance changes, and keeps the house in my net worth picture.
• Monthly report on the first Monday.
• Quarterly audit: fixes miscategorized transactions, compares spending to budget, lists every subscription, and reminds me to reconcile balances.
• January: a checklist of every tax form to expect, including the mortgage interest form, then help filing.
• Ask anytime: "what did I spend on dining?" or "project my net worth over 20 years."

Guardrails: it reads but never moves money, never changes budgets without asking, and pings my supervisor bot only for high-stakes problems.

My favorite part is the question cards. Instead of a wall of questions, it asks everything on one card:
1. "Electric ran 30% over. Raise the budget?" [Yes] [No] [Keep it at $175] [type your own]
2. "A $14.99 charge is new. What is it?" [Streaming] [Software] [Not sure] [type your own]
One tap per step and I'm done.

Template, copy and paste:
"You are my Personal Finance bot. Read my accounts in [Monarch Money / your budgeting app / CSV exports]. Each [Monday], compare actuals to my budget. Flag any bill or income that changes, missed savings transfers, low balances and stale connections; otherwise say nothing. Track my savings goals [list them] and a sinking-fund ledger for [list irregular bills]. Track my home equity [property, mortgage] and flag escrow or payment changes. Each quarter, fix miscategorized transactions, check my investment allocation and concentration, and list my subscriptions. In January, list the tax forms I should expect. Never move money or change budgets without asking. When you need my input, ask on ONE question card with steps, allow a typed answer on every step, and give Yes/No plus real alternatives."

#AI #PersonalFinance #GrokBot #MonarchMoney

text:
Amazon "lost" a $34 pair of pants I never got.

Their site said I'd be refunded "when we receive your item." I never had the item. So I handed the whole mess to my AI assistant on Grok @bot .

I sent it one rambling voice note. It pulled the order emails, rebuilt the timeline, and went into my Amazon account on its own computer.

It found the problem in minutes. Tracking said "delivery cancelled, refund coming." The return page said "drop it off first," and the refund would go to an Amazon balance, not my card. Two pages that contradicted each other, and my money stuck in the middle.

It told me not to drop anything off. Then it opened a support chat and got a promise of a refund to my card, no return needed.

Five days later, still no refund. I said "go back at them." It opened a new chat, and the agent admitted the first refund was never issued. They issued it on the spot.

Twenty minutes later I had the email: $34.23 back on my card.

My total effort was two voice messages. No hold music, no chat queue, no copy-pasting order numbers.

It's not about the $34. It's having something that sticks with the boring stuff and doesn't let it fall through the cracks.

What's the most annoying refund you've ever had to chase?
use_case_summary_en: After Amazon marked undelivered $34 pants as needing a drop-off, the user sent two voice notes to Grok Bot, which reconstructed the order, chatted with support twice, and got a $34.23 card refund.
